'''Pavel Sergeyevich Alexandrov''' ({{langx|ru|Па́вел Серге́евич Алекса́ндров}}), sometimes romanized ''Paul Alexandroff'' (7 May 1896 – 16 November 1982), was a [[Soviet Union|Soviet]] mathematician. He wrote roughly three hundred papers, making important contributions to [[set theory]] and [[topology]]. In topology, the [[Alexandroff compactification]] and the [[Alexandrov topology]] are named after him.

==Biography==
Alexandrov attended [[Moscow State University]] where he was a student of [[Dmitri Egorov]] and [[Nikolai Luzin]]. Together with [[Pavel Urysohn]], he visited the [[University of Göttingen]] in 1923 and 1924. After getting his Ph.D. in 1927, he continued to work at Moscow State University and also joined the [[Steklov Institute of Mathematics]].

He was made a member of the [[Russian Academy of Sciences]] in 1953.

=== Personal life ===
Luzin challenged Alexandrov to determine if the [[continuum hypothesis]] is true. This problem was too much for Alexandrov and he had a creative crisis at the end of 1917. The failure was a heavy blow for Alexandrov: <blockquote>"It became clear to me that the work on the continuum problem ended in a serious disaster. I also felt that I could no longer move on to mathematics and, so to speak, to the next tasks, and that some decisive turning point must come in my life." </blockquote> In 1964, the continuum hypothesis was proven to be [[Continuum hypothesis#Independence from ZFC|independent from ZFC]]. 

Alexandrov went to [[Chernihiv]], where he participated in the organisation of the drama theater: <blockquote>"I met L. V. Sobinov there, who was at that time the head of the Department of Arts of the Ukrainian People's Commissariat of Education."</blockquote>During this period, Alexandrov visited Denikin prison and was ill with [[typhus]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Sadovnichy |first=Viktor Antonovich |chapter=Aleksandr Nikolayevich Nesmeyanov (1899—1980) |language=ru |script-title=ru:О людях Московского университета |trans-title=About the people of Moscow University |edition=3rd, expanded |location=Moscow |publisher=Moscow University Publishing House |date=2019 |pages=127–133 |isbn=978-5-19-011397-6}}</ref>{{rp|p=128}}

In 1955, he signed the "Letter of Three Hundred" with criticism of [[Lysenkoism]].<ref>{{cite journal | title=To the 50th anniversary of the "Letters of the Three Hundred" | url=http://www.ihst.ru/projects/sohist/papers/internet/12_33.pdf | journal=VOGiS Bulletin | year=2005 | volume=9 | issue=1 | pages=12–33 | language=ru | archive-date=2007-10-12 | access-date=2020-12-19 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071012144507/http://www.ihst.ru/projects/sohist/papers/internet/12_33.pdf | url-status=dead }}</ref>

He was buried at the Kavezinsky cemetery of the Pushkinsky district of the Moscow region.<ref>[http://www.necropol.org/pushkinskiy-june09.html Pushkinsky district of Moscow region]</ref>

=== Private life ===
In 1921, he married {{ill|Ekaterina Romanovna Eiges|ru|Эйгес, Екатерина Романовна}}, who was a poet and memoirist, library worker and mathematician.<ref>{{Cite news |last=С.Костырко |title=Воспоминания о Сергее Есенине |url=http://magazines.russ.ru/novyi_mi/1995/9/eyges.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190705011141/http://magazines.russ.ru/novyi_mi/1995/9/eyges.html |archive-date=2019-07-05 |access-date=2025-05-03 |work=Журнальный зал |url-status=live }}</ref> However, they divorced after only a few days, since he was in fact [[Gay men|gay]], and declared:<blockquote>"Any marriage would have been a mistake for me."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Graham |first=Loren R. |title=Naming infinity: a true story of religious mysticism and mathematical creativity |last2=Kantor |first2=Jean-Michel |date=2009 |publisher=Belknap press of Harvard University press |isbn=978-0-674-03293-4 |location=Cambridge (Mass.) |pages=174}}</ref></blockquote>He then started a relationship with [[Pavel Urysohn]], with whom he shared a passion for swimming. Unfortunately, Urysohn died when they swam together in the [[Atlantic Ocean]], in [[Batz-sur-Mer]], during their vacations in August 1924.

Later, he got together with [[Andrey Kolmogorov]], and stayed with him for the rest of his life.<ref name="GrahamKantor2009">{{cite book |last1=Graham |first1=Loren R. |title=Naming infinity: a true story of religious mysticism and mathematical creativity |last2=Kantor |first2=Jean-Michel |publisher=[[Harvard University Press]] |year=2009 |isbn=978-0-674-03293-4 |page=185 |quote=The police soon learned of Kolmogorov and Alexandrov's homosexual bond, and they used that knowledge to obtain the behavior that they wished.}}</ref><ref>{{citation |last=Szpiro |first=George |title=Pricing the Future: Finance, Physics, and the 300-year Journey to the Black-Scholes Equation |page=152 |year=2011 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PFOAKB4HtF0C&pg=PA152 |publisher=Basic Books |isbn=9780465022489 |quote=It was generally known that they had a homosexual relationship, although they never acknowledged their liaison |authorlink=George Szpiro}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Gessen |first=Masha |title=Perfect Rigour: A Genius and the Mathematical Breakthrough of a Lifetime |publisher=Icon Books Ltd |year=2011 |isbn= |page=17 |quote=Kolmogorov alone among the top Soviet mathematicians avoided being drafted into the postwar military effort. His students always wondered why-and the only likely explanation seems to be Kolmogorov's homosexuality. His lifelong partner, with whom he shared a home starting in 1929, was the topologist Pavel Alexandrov.}}</ref> Looking back at their relationship, he stated: <blockquote>"In 1979 this friendship [with Kolmogorov] celebrated its fiftieth anniversary and over the whole of this half century there was not only never any breach in it, there was also never any quarrel, in all this time there was never any misunderstanding between us on any question, no matter how important for our lives and our philosophy; even when our opinions on one of these questions differed, we showed complete understanding and sympathy for the views of each other."<ref name="vitányi">{{cite journal |last1=Vitányi |first1=P.M.B. |year=1988 |title=Andrei Nikolaevich Kolmogorov |url=http://repository.cwi.nl/search/fullrecord.php?publnr=2429 |url-status=dead |journal=[[CWI Quarterly]] |publisher=Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica |volume=1 |issue=2 |pages=3–18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110718192621/http://repository.cwi.nl/search/fullrecord.php?publnr=2429 |archive-date=2011-07-18}}</ref></blockquote>

== Scientific activity ==
Alexandrov's main works are on topology, set theory, theory of functions of a real variable, geometry, calculus of variations, mathematical logic, and foundations of mathematics.<ref>{{cite book |last=Bogolyubov |first=Alexey Nikolaevich |language=uk |script-title=uk:Математики. Механики. Биографический справочник |trans-title=Mathematicians. Mechanics. Biographical reference book |location=Kyiv |publisher=Наукова думка (Scientific thought) |date=1983 |pages=127–128}}</ref>

He introduced the new concept of [[compact space|compactness]] (Alexandrov himself called it "Bicompactness", and applied the term compact to only countably compact spaces, as was customary before him). Together with P. S. Urysohn, Alexandrov showed the full meaning of this concept; in particular, he proved the first general [[metrization theorem]] and the famous compactification theorem of any locally compact Hausdorff space by adding a single point.{{sfn|Bogolyubov|1983|p=127}}

From 1923 P. S. Alexandrov began to study [[combinatorial topology]], and he managed to combine this branch of topology with general topology and significantly advance the resulting theory, which became the basis for modern [[algebraic topology]]. It was he who introduced one of the basic concepts of algebraic topology — the concept of an [[exact sequence]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Sadovnichy |first=Viktor Antonovich |chapter=Pavel Sergeyevich Alexandrov (1896—1982) |language=ru |script-title=ru:О людях Московского университета |trans-title=About the people of Moscow University |location=Moscow |publisher=Moscow University Publishing House |date=2015 |isbn=978-5-19-011041-8 |page=96}}</ref> Alexandrov also introduced the notion of a [[nerve of a covering]], which led him (independently of E. Čech) to the discovery of Alexandrov-Čech Cohomology.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Chernavsky A.V. | title = Eduard Cech (to the tenth anniversary of his death) | journal = Russian Mathematical Surveys | url = http://www.mathnet.ru/links/a3d5b2d1e3fedad97e19fffb5e23dd51/rm5200.pdf | edition = Advances in Mathematical Sciences | year = 1971 | volume = 26 | issue = 3 (159) | pages = 161–164 | language = ru | publisher = Russian Academy of Sciences | doi = 10.1070/RM1971v026n03ABEH003833 | bibcode = 1971RuMaS..26..177C | s2cid = 250873380 }}</ref>

In 1924, Alexandrov proved that in every open cover of a separable metric space, a locally finite open cover can be inscribed (this very concept, one of the key concepts in general topology, was first introduced by Alexandrov. {{sfn|Sadovnichy|2015|p=96}} In fact, this proved the paracompact nature of separable metric spaces (although the term "paracompact space" was introduced by [[Jean Dieudonné]] in 1944, and in 1948 [[Arthur Harold Stone]] showed that the requirement of separability can be abandoned).

He significantly advanced the theory of dimension. In particular, he founded the homological theory of dimension, defining its basic concepts in 1932.{{sfn|Sadovnichy|2015|p=97}} He developed methods of combinatorial research of general topological spaces, proving a number of basic laws of topological duality. In 1927, he generalized Alexander's theorem to the case of an arbitrary closed set.{{sfn|Bogolyubov|1983|pp=127–128}}

Alexandrov and [[Pavel Urysohn|P. S. Urysohn]] were the founders of the Moscow topological school, which received international recognition.{{sfn|Sadovnichy|2015|p=96}} A number of concepts and theorems of topology bear Alexandrov's name: the Alexandrov compactification, the Alexandrov-Hausdorff theorem on the cardinality of a-sets, the Alexandrov topology, and the Alexandrov-Čech homology and cohomology.

His books played an important role in the development of science and [[mathematics education]] in Russia: ''Introduction to the General Theory of Sets and Functions'', ''Combinatorial Topology'', ''Lectures on Analytical Geometry'', ''Dimension Theory'' (together with B. A. Pasynkov) and ''Introduction to Homological Dimension Theory''.

The textbook ''Topologie I'', written together with [[Heinz Hopf]] in German (Alexandroff P., Hopf H. (1935) ''Topologie'' Band 1 — Berlin) became the classic course of topology of its time.

=== The Luzin Affair ===
In 1936, Alexandrov was an active participant in the political offensive against his former mentor Luzin that is known as the [[Nikolai Luzin#The Luzin affair of 1936|Luzin affair]].

Despite the fact that P. S. Alexandrov was a student of N. N. Luzin and one of the members of the {{ill|Lusitania group|fr|Lusitania (société savante)}}, during the persecution of Luzin (the Luzin Affair), Alexandrov was one of the most active persecutors of the scientist. Relations between Luzin and Alexandrov remained very strained until the end of Luzin's life, and Alexandrov became an academician only after Luzin's death.

=== Students ===
Among the students of P. S. Alexandrov, the most famous are [[Lev Semenovich Pontryagin|Lev Pontryagin]], [[Andrey Nikolayevich Tychonoff|Andrey Tychonoff]] and [[Aleksandr Gennadievich Kurosh|Aleksandr Kurosh]].{{sfn|Bogolyubov|1983|p=128}} The older generation of his students includes L. A. Tumarkin, V. V. Nemytsky, A. N. Cherkasov, N. B. Vedenisov, G. S. Chogoshvili. The group of "Forties" includes Yu. M. Smirnov, K. A. Sitnikov, O. V. Lokutsievsky, E. F. Mishchenko, M. R. Shura-Bura. The generation of the fifties includes A.V. Arkhangelsky, B. A. Pasynkov, V. I. Ponomarev, as well as E. G. Sklyarenko and A. A. Maltsev, who were in graduate school under Yu.M. Smirnov and K. A. Sitnikov, respectively. The group of the youngest students is formed by V. V. Fedorchuk, V. I. Zaitsev and E. V. Shchepin.
